title: N-Dimensional Arrays
body:
The N-dimensional array is the fundamental building block in numerical computing libraries, e.g., NumPy and SciPy. It is the core dense data structure and many advanced numerical functions are built on top of it, including linear algebra, optimisation, and algorithmic differentiation. In fact, the rest of this book is built upon it. In this chapter, we introduce the Ndarray module and its core functions. We then pay particular attention to its two key and frequently used functionalities: slicing and broadcasting. Finally, we briefly explain the concept of a tensor, similar to but different from the N-dimensional array.

Running the examples

Source: code/chap05_ndarray
Run: python3 scripts/run_chapter05.py

In utop, load this setup and follow the examples in order:

OCAML
Owl_stats_prng.init 75;;
let book_matrix_printer formatter value =
  Owl_pretty.print_dsnda ~max_row:8 ~max_col:8 ~formatter value;;
#install_printer book_matrix_printer;;

The examples of compatible and incompatible array shapes in Sect. 5.3 are illustrations rather than executable OCaml code.

5.1 Ndarray

An N-dimensional array (a.k.a. ndarray) is the most fundamental data type in a numerical library for building scientific computing applications. Scalar-based computations are easy to understand but can become cumbersome when working with large arrays. Ndarray is the key data structure in many mainstream numerical libraries and software, including NumPy, Julia, and TensorFlow. This chapter introduces Owl’s Ndarray, a fundamental module in OCaml numerical computing, and the basic functionalities it provides.

5.1.1 Types

We begin by looking at the data types used in Ndarray, which is built directly on top of OCaml’s native Bigarray data structure. The Bigarray module is used to express large, multi-dimensional numerical arrays, and is designed to enable efficient sharing of large numerical arrays between OCaml code and C or FORTRAN numerical libraries. More specifically, Ndarray is defined based on the Bigarray.Genarray submodule:

OCAML SESSION
type ('a, 'b) t = ('a, 'b, Bigarray.c_layout) Bigarray.Genarray.t

The type parameters of Genarray.t specify the OCaml element type, storage kind, and memory layout of a multi-dimensional array. Based on different combinations of (’a, ’b), Ndarray supports four combinations of number type and precision: single precision float (S), double precision float (D), single precision complex number (C), and double precision complex number (Z). These are all accessed by modules Ndarray.S, Ndarray.D, etc. In what follows, unless otherwise stated, we will use the double precision Ndarray.D module which is aliased to the Arr module.

The Ndarray module is designed to use row-major layout (c_layout) in its implementation. This indicates that adjacent elements along the last dimension are contiguous in memory, compared to FORTRAN layout where this holds along the first dimension. From the perspective of designing Owl, our reasons for making this decision are as follows.

  • Mixing memory layouts causes bugs. In particular, indexing in FORTRAN starts from 1 while indexing in C starts from 0, and many native OCaml data structures such as Array and List all index from 0. So sticking with C-layout avoids many clashes when using Owl.
  • Supporting both layouts adds considerable complexity when implementing the underlying functions. Code which performs well on one layout may not do well on the other, and so many functions would require different implementations for different layouts. This would add much complexity and significantly increase the code base for only marginal benefits.
  • Ndarray has rather different design principles compared to Bigarray. The latter serves as a basic tool for operating on a chunk of memory living outside the OCaml heap, and facilitates exchanging data between different libraries (including FORTRAN ones). The numerical library we use here focuses on providing high-level numerical functions allowing programmers to write concise analytical code. The simple design and small code base outweigh the benefits of supporting both layouts.

Note that in Owl, a matrix is just a special case of an N-dimensional array, and you can add a matrix and a 2-dimensional ndarray of compatible shape and element kind. In fact many functions in the Matrix module simply call the same functions in Ndarray.

5.1.2 Ndarray Creation and Properties

We start by introducing several groups of key functions provided by Ndarray. The first group is the creation functions that generate dense data structures. The most frequently used are probably empty, create, zeros, and ones. These functions return ndarrays of the specified shape.

Note that the empty function allocates storage without initialising its elements. This avoids the cost of filling the array, but its contents must be set before use. The other three are hopefully self-explanatory: zeros and ones fill the allocated memory with zeros and ones respectively, whereas the create function fills the memory with the specified value.

If you need random numbers, you can use another three creation functions that return ndarrays in which the elements follow specified distributions: uniform, gaussian, and bernoulli. You can provide optional distribution parameters, e.g., μ and σ for a Gaussian distribution; their defaults are 0 and 1 respectively.

We sometimes need to generate numbers equally spaced between bounds, for example when generating intervals or plotting figures. The sequential and linspace functions serve that purpose, producing ndarrays filled with evenly spaced numbers. The former takes a shape and optional starting value and step, which need not be an integer; the latter takes endpoints and a number of points.

If these do not satisfy your requirements, Ndarray provides more flexible means that give you more control over initialisation via the init and init_nd functions. The first only passes 1-dimensional indices to a user-defined function, while the second passes n-dimensional indices and incurs the extra cost of computing them. The example below creates an ndarray where all the elements are even numbers:

OCAML SESSION
# let x = Arr.init [|6;8|] (fun i -> 2. *. (float_of_int i));;
val x : Owl.Arr.arr =

   C0 C1 C2 C3 C4 C5 C6 C7
R0  0  2  4  6  8 10 12 14
R1 16 18 20 22 24 26 28 30
R2 32 34 36 38 40 42 44 46
R3 48 50 52 54 56 58 60 62
R4 64 66 68 70 72 74 76 78
R5 80 82 84 86 88 90 92 94

After creation, there are various functions that obtain the properties of the ndarray. For example, given ndarrays x and y, the following functions are commonly used:

  • shape x returns the shape of x
  • num_dims x returns the number of dimensions of x
  • nth_dim x n returns the size of the n-th dimension of x
  • numel x returns the number of elements in x
  • nnz x returns the number of non-zero elements in x
  • density x returns the fraction of non-zero elements in x
  • size_in_bytes x returns the size of the element storage of x in bytes
  • same_shape x y checks whether x and y have the same shape
  • kind x returns the element kind of ndarray x

5.1.3 Map, Fold, and Scan

Three typical generic operations are worth special attention: map, fold, and scan. The map function transforms one ndarray to another by applying the provided function to every element in the original ndarray. For example, the code below:

OCAML
let y = Arr.map (fun a -> a +. 1.) x;;

adds 1 to every element in the ndarray x, then returns a new ndarray y. The map function in Ndarray returns a fresh array without modifying the input, provided the supplied function does not itself mutate it. If your transformation function needs the index of the element being operated on, the mapi function passes its flattened, zero-based index; mapi_nd passes an array of coordinates instead.

The fold function is sometimes referred to as “reduction” in other languages. It has a named parameter called axis that specifies the axis along which you want to fold the given ndarray. The axis parameter is optional. If you do not specify one, the ndarray will be folded along all the dimensions into a single element (that is, a one-dimensional ndarray of length one). The fold function folds from the left, and requires an initial value for the folding. The code below demonstrates how to implement your own sum function. It adds the elements along the selected axis and returns an ndarray by folding the function +. with an initial value of 0.

OCAML
let sum ?axis x = Arr.fold ?axis ( +. ) 0. x;;

The functions sum, sum’, prod, prod’, min, min’, mean, and mean’ all perform reductions with various functions. The prime ending indicates that the function returns a number rather than an ndarray. As with map, if indices are required, the foldi function passes in 1-dimensional indices.

Finally, scan is analogous to a combination of map and fold, accumulating values along the specified axis but not changing the shape of the input. For example, consider generating a cumulative distribution function from a discrete probability mass function, as introduced in Chap. 3. Several functions belong to this group, such as cumsum, cumprod, cummin, cummax. Again, the scani function accepts cumulative functions that need index information.

Many common operations on ndarrays can be decomposed as a series of map, fold, and scan operations. The map and reduce operations also inspire the MapReduce programming model [4]. The Ndarray module includes a comprehensive set of vectorised element-wise mathematical functions. This means you can apply them directly on an ndarray and the function will be automatically applied to every element in the ndarray. For binary math operators, there are add, sub, mul, etc. For unary operators, there are sin, cos, abs, etc.

Conceptually, all of these can be implemented using just map, fold, and scan. For example, to make your own vectorised sin function, you need only execute Arr.map sin x. However, this may well be slower than the native vectorised functions, which are implemented in C code for efficiency.

5.1.4 Comparison Functions

The comparison functions in Ndarray can be divided into several groups.

The first group compares two ndarrays and returns a boolean value, such as equal, less, and greater. The second compares two ndarrays element by element and returns a 0-1 ndarray of the broadcast result shape, with 1 where the predicate is satisfied and 0 otherwise: elt_equal, elt_not_equal, etc. The third is similar to the first, but compares an ndarray with a scalar value, and returns a boolean: equal_scalar, not_equal_scalar, etc. The fourth is similar to the second but compares an ndarray with a scalar, and returns a 0-1 ndarray: elt_equal_scalar, elt_less_scalar, etc.

We generally recommend using the appropriate operators rather than calling these functions directly as it leads to more concise code.

For example, the following code shows two ways to retain all elements greater than 0.5 and set the rest to 0 in an ndarray of finite values.

OCAML
let y = Arr.map (fun a -> if a > 0.5 then a else 0.) x;;
let z = Arr.((x >.$ 0.5) * x);;

The operator version leads to more concise code and can be faster because the loops run in C rather than OCaml, at the price of an additional temporary mask. The actual performance depends on the input size and environment. Please refer to the Appendix A to learn about all these operators.

5.1.5 Iteration Functions

As with native OCaml arrays, you can use iter and iteri to iterate over all the elements in an ndarray. One common use case is to check if one or more predicates are satisfied and there is a special set of iteration functions to help you in this task: is_zero, is_positive, is_negative, is_nonpositive, is_nonnegative, and is_normal, etc. All take an ndarray as input and return a boolean value.

More complex predicates can be tested using the three functions exists, not_exists, and for_all while passing in arbitrarily complicated functions that return a boolean. While these functions only tell us whether the predicates are met or not, the filter function can return the 1-dimensional indices of those elements that satisfy the predicates.

Processing flattened 1-dimensional indices avoids the cost of converting them to n-dimensional indices. However, if you do need n-dimensional indices, you can use the functions ind and i1d to convert between flattened and n-dimensional indices. Both are defined in the Owl.Utils module. Note that you need to pass in the original ndarray because the shape information is required for calculating index conversion.

5.1.6 Manipulation Functions

In addition to those we have introduced, the Ndarray module contains many useful functions to manipulate ndarrays. For example, you can tile and repeat an ndarray along a specified axis. Let’s first create a sequential ndarray.

OCAML SESSION
# let x = Arr.sequential [|3;4|];;
val x : Owl.Arr.arr =

   C0 C1 C2 C3
R0  0  1  2  3
R1  4  5  6  7
R2  8  9 10 11

The code below tiles x twice along each dimension.

OCAML SESSION
# let y = Arr.tile x [|2;2|];;
val y : Owl.Arr.arr =

   C0 C1 C2 C3 C4 C5 C6 C7
R0  0  1  2  3  0  1  2  3
R1  4  5  6  7  4  5  6  7
R2  8  9 10 11  8  9 10 11
R3  0  1  2  3  0  1  2  3
R4  4  5  6  7  4  5  6  7
R5  8  9 10 11  8  9 10 11

The repeat function replicates each element in its adjacent cell along the specified dimension, as shown below.

OCAML SESSION
# let z = Arr.repeat x [|2;1|];;
val z : Owl.Arr.arr =

   C0 C1 C2 C3
R0  0  1  2  3
R1  0  1  2  3
R2  4  5  6  7
R3  4  5  6  7
R4  8  9 10 11
R5  8  9 10 11

You can also expand the dimensionality of an ndarray, or squeeze out dimensions having only one element, or pad elements around an existing ndarray, using the functions expand, squeeze, and pad.

Another two useful functions are concatenate and split. The concatenate function allows concatenation of an array of ndarrays along the specified axis, given that the dimensions other than that on which they are concatenated are equal. There are two operators associated with concatenation for matrices: @|| concatenates horizontally (i.e. along axis 1); and @= for concatenating vertically (i.e. along axis 0). split is then the inverse operation of concatenation. You can also sort an ndarray with sort, which returns a sorted copy; sort_ modifies it in place.

Another feature we will use frequently in this book is to convert between ndarrays and normal arrays using conversion functions of_array and to_array.

5.1.7 Serialisation

In data analysis tasks we often need to save temporary results and later reload them. This process requires the serialisation and de-serialisation functions save and load.

With the help of the tool npy-ocaml1, we can save and load files in the NPY binary file format from NumPy. It stores all of the shape and data type information necessary to reconstruct the array correctly, even on another machine with a different architecture. It is a widely used serialisation format in numerical tasks. The corresponding functions are save_npy and load_npy; the stored element kind must match the module used to load the array. By using these functions, we can easily interact with the Python-world data from OCaml.

5.2 Slicing

Slicing in ndarray is the operation that extracts part of an ndarray or a matrix according to a slice definition, an index list that indicates which indices should be accessed and in what order for each dimension of the value being sliced. Indexing and slicing are arguably the most important ndarray functions in any numerical library. Owl’s flexible design significantly simplifies the code, allowing us to write concise algorithms. In this section we will introduce ndarray basic and fancy slicing, which differ in how the slice is defined.

5.2.1 Slice Definition

In basic slicing, each dimension in the slice definition is specified by a list of up to three integers, [start;stop;step]. Ndarray provides two functions get_slice and set_slice to retrieve and assign slice values respectively. Both accept an int list list as the slice definition, where every list element in the int list list is assumed to be a range. For example, [ []; [2]; [-1;3] ] is equivalent to the full slice definition [ R []; R [2]; R [-1;3] ] in fancy slicing notation shown below.

OCAML SESSION
type index =
  Owl_types_common.index =
    I of int
  | L of int list
  | R of int list

The fancy slicing is defined by an index list that uses three type constructors. I simply specifies a numeric index, so [ I 2; I 5 ] returns a 1 x 1 matrix containing the element at position (2, 5). L specifies a list of indices, so [ I 2; L [5;3] ] returns a 1 x 2 matrix with the elements at (2, 5) and (2, 3) in the original matrix. Finally, R specifies a range of indices. Similarly to get_slice, the get_fancy s x retrieves a slice of x defined by s, whereas set_fancy s x y assigns the slice of x defined by s according to values in y. Note that y must have the same shape as that defined by s. For example, these two slices of x are equivalent:

OCAML
let x = Arr.sequential [|10; 10; 10|];;
Arr.get_slice [ []; [0;8]; [3;9;2] ] x;;
Arr.get_fancy [ R[]; R[0;8]; R[3;9;2] ] x;;

Note that both get_slice and get_fancy return a copy. NumPy basic slicing returns a view, whereas its advanced indexing returns a copy. In Owl, set_slice and set_fancy modify the original data in place.

The operators for indexing and slicing are built on the extended indexing operators introduced in OCaml 4.06. In the slicing system, they are used as aliases for the slicing functions we introduced above:

  • .%{ } : get
  • .%{ }<- : set
  • .${ } : get_slice
  • .${ }<- : set_slice
  • .!{ } : get_fancy
  • .!{ }<- : set_fancy

For example, we can use .%{ } for indexing as follows:

OCAML
open Arr;;
let x = sequential [|10; 10; 10|] in
let a = x.%{2; 3; 4} in
x.%{2; 3; 4} <- 111.;;

Another example uses the .!{ } operator for fancy slicing:

OCAML
open Arr;;
let x = sequential [|10; 10; 10|] in
let a = x.!{L [2;2;1]; R [6;-1]; I 5} in
let b = zeros (shape a) in
x.!{L [2;2;1]; R [6;-1]; I 5} <- b;;

5.2.2 Conventions and Examples

These definitions of slicing may look complicated. The following rules can help write correct slice definitions. These conventions can be equally applied to both basic and fancy slicing. They resemble those in NumPy, but Owl includes the stop index when reached by the step, infers a descending step when needed, and retains singleton dimensions. If you already know how to slice n-dimensional arrays in NumPy, you should find them easy to follow.

  • Rule #1: The format of the range definition follows R [ start; stop; step ]. start specifies the starting index, stop specifies the inclusive stopping bound, and step specifies the step size. You do not have to specify all three variables in the definition; see the following rules.
  • Rule #2: All three variables start, stop, and step can take both positive and negative values, but step is not allowed to be zero. Positive step indicates that indices will be visited in increasing order from start to stop; and vice versa.
  • Rule #3: For start and stop variables, non-negative values refer to a specific index while a negative value “a” will be translated into n + a where n is the size of that dimension. E.g., [ -1; 0 ] indicates the slice from the last index to the first.
  • Rule #4: If you pass in an empty list R [], this will be expanded into [ 0; n - 1; 1 ] which means all the indices will be visited in increasing order with step size 1.
  • Rule #5: If you only specify one variable such as [ start ], get_slice assumes that you will take one specific index by automatically extending it into [ start; start; 1 ]. As we can see, start and stop are the same, with step size 1.
  • Rule #6: If you only specify two variables, the get_slice function assumes they are [ start; stop ] which defines the range of indices. However, how get_slice will expand this slice definition depends. After converting negative indices, get_slice visits indices in different orders. If start <= stop, it will be expanded to [ start; stop; 1 ]; otherwise it will be expanded to [ start; stop; -1 ].
  • Rule #7: It is not necessary to specify all the definitions for all the dimensions: the get_slice function will also expand it by assuming you will take all the data in higher dimensions. E.g., suppose x has the shape [|2;3;4|], if we define the slice as [ [0] ], get_slice will expand the definition into [ [0]; []; [] ].

That’s all the rules.

Let’s look at some examples. All are based on an 8×8 array, initialised explicitly below. The first is shown in Fig. 5.1(a), taking one column of the matrix using both basic and fancy slicing:

OCAML SESSION
# let x = Arr.sequential [|8;8|];;
val x : Owl.Arr.arr =

   C0 C1 C2 C3 C4 C5 C6 C7
R0  0  1  2  3  4  5  6  7
R1  8  9 10 11 12 13 14 15
R2 16 17 18 19 20 21 22 23
R3 24 25 26 27 28 29 30 31
R4 32 33 34 35 36 37 38 39
R5 40 41 42 43 44 45 46 47
R6 48 49 50 51 52 53 54 55
R7 56 57 58 59 60 61 62 63
# Arr.get_slice [ []; [2]  ] x;;
- : Owl.Arr.arr =

   C0
R0  2
R1 10
R2 18
R3 26
R4 34
R5 42
R6 50
R7 58
# Arr.get_fancy [ R[]; I 2 ] x;;
- : Owl.Arr.arr =

   C0
R0  2
R1 10
R2 18
R3 26
R4 34
R5 42
R6 50
R7 58

The second in Fig. 5.1(b) is similar, but retrieves part of a row, again using both methods.

OCAML SESSION
# Arr.get_slice [ [2]; [4; 6] ] x;;
- : Owl.Arr.arr =
   C0 C1 C2
R0 20 21 22
# Arr.get_fancy [ I 2; R [4; 6] ] x;;
- : Owl.Arr.arr =
   C0 C1 C2
R0 20 21 22

The next example in Fig. 5.2(a) is a bit more complex. It chooses certain rows, and then chooses columns using a fixed step of 2, via fancy slicing:

OCAML SESSION
# Arr.get_fancy [ L [3; 5]; R [1; 7; 2] ] x;;
- : Owl.Arr.arr =
   C0 C1 C2 C3
R0 25 27 29 31
R1 41 43 45 47

Finally, the last example in Fig. 5.2(b) obtains a sub-matrix in a similar manner to examples 1 and 2, using negative integers as indices.

OCAML SESSION
# Arr.get_fancy [ L [-2; -1]; R [-3; -2] ] x;;
- : Owl.Arr.arr =
   C0 C1
R0 53 54
R1 61 62

5.2.3 Advanced Usage

There are more advanced usages of slicing besides what we have just seen, which we will demonstrate in this section. Based on the same input matrix x, these examples vary the index s in Mat.get_slice s x. Mat is the matrix module built on Ndarray; all the following examples also hold for ndarrays.

  • []: take all the elements
  • [ [2]; [] ]: take row 2
  • [ [2] ]: take row 2, but only specify the first dimension
  • [ [1;3] ]: take from row 1 to 3
  • [ [3;1] ]: take from row 3 to 1, same as the example above but in reverse order

Let’s look at some more complicated examples.

  • [ [1;3]; [3;5] ] take from row 1 to 3 and column 3 to 5, so a sub-matrix of x
  • [ [1;-1]; [] ] take from row 1 to the last row
  • [ [0;-1;2] ] take the rows with even indices, i.e., 0;2;4;6
  • [ []; [1;-1;2] ] take columns with odd indices, i.e.,1;3;5;7
  • [ [-1;0] ] reverse all the rows of x
  • [ [-1;0]; [-1;0] ] reverse all the elements of x, same as applying reverse function
  • [ [-2]; [0;-1;3] ] take the second last row, at column indices 0, 3, and 6

The following examples show how to use slicing to achieve some even more complicated operations. We use a 5×5 sequential matrix for illustration.

OCAML SESSION
# let x = Mat.sequential 5 5;;
val x : Owl.Mat.mat =

   C0 C1 C2 C3 C4
R0  0  1  2  3  4
R1  5  6  7  8  9
R2 10 11 12 13 14
R3 15 16 17 18 19
R4 20 21 22 23 24

In the first example, the reverse function treats a matrix as a one-dimensional vector and reverses its elements. This operation is equivalent to flipping in both vertical and horizontal directions.

OCAML SESSION
let reverse x = Mat.get_slice [ [-1;0]; [-1;0] ] x;;

# reverse x;;
- : Owl.Arr.arr =

   C0 C1 C2 C3 C4
R0 24 23 22 21 20
R1 19 18 17 16 15
R2 14 13 12 11 10
R3  9  8  7  6  5
R4  4  3  2  1  0

The second function rotates a matrix 90 degrees clockwise. As we can see, slicing leads to very concise code.

OCAML SESSION
let rotate90 x = Mat.(transpose x |> get_slice [ [];[-1;0] ]);;

# rotate90 x;;
- : Owl.Mat.mat =

   C0 C1 C2 C3 C4
R0 20 15 10  5  0
R1 21 16 11  6  1
R2 22 17 12  7  2
R3 23 18 13  8  3
R4 24 19 14  9  4

The last function cshift performs a right circular shift along the columns of a matrix.

OCAML
let cshift x n =
  let columns = Mat.col_num x in
  if columns = 0 then Mat.copy x
  else
    let n = ((n mod columns) + columns) mod columns in
    let indices = List.init columns (fun i -> (i - n + columns) mod columns) in
    Mat.get_fancy [R []; L indices] x;;
let _ = cshift x 0;;

Applying this to the previous x should produce the following output:

OCAML SESSION
# cshift x 2;;
- : Owl.Mat.mat =

   C0 C1 C2 C3 C4
R0  3  4  0  1  2
R1  8  9  5  6  7
R2 13 14 10 11 12
R3 18 19 15 16 17
R4 23 24 20 21 22

5.3 Broadcasting

We now introduce the broadcasting operation. In contrast to indexing and slicing which must be explicitly invoked, broadcasting is usually implicitly invoked when certain conditions are met. This often simplifies code but can sometimes make debugging more complicated.

Many binary mathematical operators take two ndarrays as inputs, e.g., add, sub, etc. In the trivial case, the inputs should have exactly the same shape. However, we often operate on two ndarrays whose shapes do not match. Implicitly extending compatible dimensions of either input to a common shape is called broadcasting.

Broadcasting can save unnecessary memory allocation. For example, assume we have a 1000×500 matrix x that contains 1000 samples each having 500 features. We want to add a bias vector v of shape 1×500 to each feature. As the shapes of x and v do not match, one approach is to tile v so that it has the same shape as that of x.

OCAML
let x = Mat.uniform 1000 500;;
let v = Mat.uniform 1 500;;
let u = Mat.tile v [|1000;1|];;
Mat.(x + u);;

The code above works but uses considerable memory for temporary values. High memory consumption is not desirable, particularly when running on resource-constrained devices. So we can use broadcasting to add x and v directly, without using the tile operation. The returned result is of the same shape as x.

However, the shapes of two inputs cannot be arbitrarily different in broadcasting, but are subject to some constraints. The rule is much simpler than in slicing: given two matrices/ndarrays of the same dimensionality, for each dimension, one of the following two conditions must hold: either both sizes are equal, or one size is 1.

Here are some valid shapes where broadcasting can be applied between x and y.

OCAML SESSION
  x : [| 2; 1; 3 |]    y : [| 1; 1; 1 |]
  x : [| 2; 1; 3 |]    y : [| 2; 1; 1 |]
  x : [| 2; 1; 3 |]    y : [| 2; 3; 1 |]
  ...

Here are some invalid shapes that violate the constraint above and prevent broadcasting.

OCAML SESSION
  x : [| 2; 1; 3 |]    y : [| 1; 1; 2 |]
  x : [| 2; 1; 3 |]    y : [| 3; 1; 1 |]
  x : [| 2; 1; 3 |]    y : [| 3; 1; 1 |]
  ...

What if y has lower dimensionality than x? E.g., x has the shape [|2;3;4;5|] whereas y has the shape [|4;5|]. In this case, y’s dimensionality is expanded to the same number as x’s. Technically, two ndarrays are aligned at their last dimensions. In other words, this is done by prepending 1s to the shape of y, making the new shape of y [|1;1;4;5|]. You can try expand by yourself, as shown below.

OCAML SESSION
# let y = Arr.sequential [|4;5|];;
val y : Owl.Arr.arr =

   C0 C1 C2 C3 C4
R0  0  1  2  3  4
R1  5  6  7  8  9
R2 10 11 12 13 14
R3 15 16 17 18 19
# let y' = Arr.expand y 4;;
val y' : Owl.Arr.arr =

         C0 C1 C2 C3 C4
R[0,0,0]  0  1  2  3  4
R[0,0,1]  5  6  7  8  9
R[0,0,2] 10 11 12 13 14
R[0,0,3] 15 16 17 18 19
# Arr.shape y';;
- : int array = [|1; 1; 4; 5|]

Next we show three broadcasting examples based on matrices, using both illustrations and code, so that you can better understand how the shapes are extended in broadcasting. The first example in Fig. 5.3 is a vector multiplied by a scalar.

OCAML
let a = Arr.sequential [|1;3|];;
Arr.mul_scalar a 3.;;

The second example in Fig. 5.4 is adding a matrix and a vector.

OCAML
let b0 = Arr.sequential [|3;3|];;
let b1 = Arr.sequential ~a:1. [|1;3|];;
Arr.add b0 b1;;

The third example in Fig. 5.5 is adding a column vector and a row vector.

OCAML
let c0 = Arr.sequential [|3;1|];;
let c1 = Arr.copy b1;;
Arr.add c0 c1;;

The broadcasting operation is transparent so it will be automatically applied if the shapes of two operands do not match and the constraints are met. Operations in Owl that support broadcasting include:

  • basic computation: add, sub, mul, div, pow;
  • comparison operation: elt_equal, elt_not_equal, elt_less, elt_greater, elt_less_equal, elt_greater_equal;
  • other: min2, max2, atan2, hypot, fmod.

5.4 Tensors

We finish this chapter by briefly introducing the concept of tensor. Many people use tensor and n-dimensional array interchangeably but there are differences between them. A tensor can be represented by an array of components in a chosen basis, but those components must also obey certain transformation rules. For example, in a three-dimensional vector space we might have a vector with components [0, 1, 2]. We can find each component using a single index. This vector is an object in the space, and it stays the same even if we change the basis. If we do change the basis, its components must be updated accordingly. In this way we represent tensors as ndarrays, but a stored array alone does not specify how its components transform. In numerical libraries, the word tensor is also commonly used simply to mean a multi-dimensional array.

Consider a single vector with component column v in a basis e. We can change the basis to ẽ via an invertible matrix A, with ẽj = ∑ ⁡ ieiAji. The component column in the new basis is then ṽ = A−1v, written as:

ṽi = ∑ jBjivj. (5.1)

Here B = A−1. We call these components contravariant because they transform inversely to the basis change. Note that we use superscripts to denote them.

As a comparison, think about a linear functional represented by a row α, so that 𝛼𝑣 is a scalar. Such functionals form the dual vector space. To keep 𝛼𝑣 unchanged under the same basis change, the row must transform as α~ = 𝛼𝐴, or in components:

α~j = ∑ iAjiα i.

The functional is called a covector, and its components are denoted with subscripts. We can further extend this to matrices. Consider a linear mapping from the vector space to itself, represented by a matrix L. With the change of basis, the map remains the same, but its matrix becomes L~ = 𝐵𝐿𝐴, or:

Lji~ = ∑ 𝑘𝑙BkiL lkA jl.

Again, note that we use both a superscript and a subscript for the linear map L, since its components have one contravariant index and one covariant index.

We can further extend this process to tensors with multiple contravariant and covariant indices. A tensor T is an object independent of the basis, while its components transform as shown in Eq. 5.2. Here 𝑖𝑗𝑘… are the contravariant indices and 𝑟𝑠𝑡… are the covariant indices.

T𝑥𝑦𝑧…𝑎𝑏𝑐…~ = ∑ 𝑖𝑗𝑘…𝑟𝑠𝑡…BiaB jbB kc…T 𝑟𝑠𝑡…𝑖𝑗𝑘… A xrA ysA zt… (5.2)

One of the important operations on tensors is the tensor contraction, applied to two tensors producing a third tensor through a summation process. Suppose we have tensor A𝑖𝑗𝑘𝑎𝑏𝑐 and B𝑟𝑠𝑡𝑘𝑙, and you can see that a pair of indices, one covariant of A and one contravariant of B, are labelled with the same letter k. This implies a summation over those two indices. As a result of summation, a new tensor C𝑖𝑗𝑟𝑠𝑡𝑎𝑏𝑐𝑙 has the indices of the tensors A and B except for the pair of indices over which the contraction operations took place. In this example, the contraction can be expressed as:

C𝑖𝑗𝑟𝑠𝑡𝑎𝑏𝑐𝑙 = ∑ kA𝑖𝑗𝑘𝑎𝑏𝑐B 𝑟𝑠𝑡𝑘𝑙.

We can compute such contractions using the contract2 function in the Ndarray module. It takes an array of int * int tuples specifying pairs of zero-based axes in the two input ndarrays; paired axes must have equal sizes.

OCAML
let x = Mat.uniform 3 4;;
let y = Mat.uniform 4 5;;

let z1 = Mat.dot x y;;
let z2 = Arr.contract2 [|(1,0)|] x y;;

Tensor contraction is not limited to matrices. For example, we have two three-dimensional arrays A and B, and aim to compute the matrix C so that:

Cji = ∑ h𝑘 Ah𝑘iB j𝑘h (5.3)

The implementation is similar:

OCAML
let x = Arr.sequential [|3;4;5|];;
let y = Arr.sequential [|4;3;2|];;
let z1 = Arr.contract2 [|(0, 1); (1, 0)|] x y;;

The pairs mean that axis 0 of x is contracted with axis 1 of y, and axis 1 of x with axis 0 of y. Here x stores Ah𝑘i in the order (h,k,i) and y stores Bj𝑘h in the order (k,h,j), leaving a result of shape [|5;2|]. We can verify Eq. 5.3 with the naive contraction summation below, and then check if the two results z1 and z2 are the same.

OCAML
let z2 = Arr.zeros [|5;2|];;

let _ =
  for h = 0 to 2 do
    for k = 0 to 3 do
      for i = 0 to 4 do
        for j = 0 to 1 do
          let r = (Arr.get x [|h;k;i|]) *.
            (Arr.get y [|k;h;j|]) in
          Arr.set z2 [|i;j|] ((Arr.get z2 [|i;j|]) +. r)
        done
      done
    done
  done;;

Tensor contraction can also express the convolution operations we will introduce in the signal and neural network chapters.

In brief, convolution is a mathematical way of combining two signals to form a third. Each discrete signal can be represented as a vector, matrix, or ndarray. We will see that convolution is a central operation in convolutional neural networks, and it can be expressed as a series of contraction computations.

As to the implementation, both tensor contraction and discrete convolution can be implemented using general matrix multiplication, or GEMM, a core functionality of BLAS. As we introduced in Chap. 4, GEMM is efficiently implemented in various highly optimised numerical libraries such as OpenBLAS and MKL. To achieve efficiency, tensor contraction implementations can use axis permutations and reshaping to transform contractions into GEMM. Note that using BLAS operations to implement tensor contraction may incur performance and storage overhead. High-performance implementation of the contraction operation has been a research topic in computation related fields [2, 3].

Contraction can also be used to implement other operations that might initially seem unrelated to matrix multiplication. For example, it can be applied to a single ndarray to sum along a diagonal using the contract1 function, as the code below demonstrates.

OCAML SESSION
# let x = Arr.sequential [|2;2;3|];;
val x : Owl.Arr.arr =

       C0 C1 C2
R[0,0]  0  1  2
R[0,1]  3  4  5
R[1,0]  6  7  8
R[1,1]  9 10 11
# let y = Arr.contract1 [|(0,1)|] x;;
val y : Owl.Arr.arr =
  C0 C1 C2
R  9 11 13

Many tensor operations involve summation over particular indices. Therefore in applications such as linear algebra and physics, the Einstein notation is used to simplify expressions [1, Chap. 1, pp. 5–7]. In the mixed-index convention used here, it omits the summation symbol for an index appearing twice in a term, once as a superscript and once as a subscript; no index may occur three times or more in a term. For example, the matrix multiplication notation Cji = ∑ ⁡ kAkiBjk can be simplified to Cji = AkiBjk. The free indices i and j remain on both sides. Eq. 5.2 can also be greatly simplified in this way.

Tensor calculus is frequently used in physics and engineering, in areas including relativity, quantum physics, and fluid mechanics. More details about tensor calculus are beyond the scope of this book, and we refer readers to work such as Dullemond and Peeters [1] for a deeper understanding of this topic.

5.5 Summary

The N-dimensional array is the most fundamental data type in numerical computing, and we will use it throughout this book. This chapter explained the details of Owl’s Ndarray module, including creation, property extraction, manipulation, serialisation, and so on. We also introduced slicing and broadcasting of ndarrays thoroughly. Mastering these topics requires practice, and this chapter provides many examples. We finished this chapter by briefly discussing the difference between a tensor and an ndarray.
